speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Health with regard to individuals who completed their primary vaccine course with non-mRNA vaccines (a) how many of these individuals’ fully-vaccinated status will expire by 14 February 2022; (b) whether those who are medically ineligible for mRNA vaccines can receive a booster dose of a non-mRNA vaccine; and (c) if not, when will non-mRNA boosters be made available.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what are the considerations for not making the Sinovac-CoronaVac and Sinopharm vaccines generally available to children and adolescents, except adolescents who are not medically eligible for the Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty vaccine; and (b) whether the Ministry has plans to make at least one non-mRNA vaccine generally available to children under 18 in order to maximise the vaccination rate of the Singapore population.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The use of the Sinovac-CoronaVac vaccine under NVP is only for persons aged 18 and above, as the vaccine manufacturer did not include children and adolescents when filing for interim authorisation of the vaccine under the Health Sciences Authority (HSA)’s Pandemic Special Access Route (PSAR).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Both Sinovac-CoronaVac and the Sinopharm vaccines are also not currently recommended for routine use in persons aged below 18 by the World Health Organization.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Notwithstanding the manufacturer’s filing on the use of the vaccine, limited data from the Sinovac-CoronaVac vaccine manufacturer’s early Phase I and II trials in healthy children and adolescents aged three to 17 do not show safety concerns and we recognise the need for alternative vaccines for persons medically ineligible for the currently approved vaccine in this age group.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: SAM is, therefore, part of a research study which, under our current regulatory framework, enabled the administration of the Sinovac vaccine to an age group outside the scope of PSAR approval.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In January 2022, the programme was further extended to eligible children aged five to 11, after the data from the older age group indicated that the safety profile of the vaccine was generally consistent with that of other registered vaccines used in immunisation against other diseases.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOH is working to bring in other non-mRNA options for those who are medically ineligible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Novavax recently released data that the vaccine was found to be 80% effective against COVID-19 in a late-stage trial in adolescents aged 12 to 17 in the United States when the Delta variant was the dominant strain.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: HSA and MOH will evaluate the data from this study and will continue to monitor for more data on its efficacy and safety in children and adolescents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We hope that the initial doses of the Novavax COVID-19 vaccine will arrive in Singapore within a matter of months, provided that there are no disruptions to the shipment schedule.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Meanwhile, those who are medically eligible are encouraged to take the available mRNA vaccines as they offer more optimal protection.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have a related supplementary question on COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How are the healthcare workers and healthcare system coping with the increased number of infected cases from the Omicron wave?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We had earlier said that, at its peak, we may reach 15,000 to 20,000 cases a day or even more.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is not increasing at three times multiples anymore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But whether cases will go up further, I think that is a possibility and we should be prepared for that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Having said that, as we have always explained, what is important now is not so much the topline infection numbers but how that translates into disease severity and impact on our healthcare capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yesterday, there were a few Written Questions on this topic, and we put out some responses to those.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By and large, our healthcare system is coping well.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will give an example – the ICU beds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At its peak, during the Delta wave, we had 171 ICU beds occupied, out of a capacity of 200-plus, close to 300.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The week before, at one point, it reached 30 and it actually came down and it is now 23.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we see it hobbling between 20 and 30.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So long as we maintain that, ICU is in good shape.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you look at those who need oxygen supplementation, those who require hospitalisation, the healthcare system is coping.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I think where we face pressure now is not on the clinical side of healthcare but on the operational side of healthcare because the number of calls from patients to our hotline is increasing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fortunately, we have the help of many public agencies like CPF Board, and SAF stood up a fairly big team to support the operations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we are able to answer well over 90% of the calls without them dropping.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the GPs are facing quite a bit of pressure.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you go to our community GP clinics, you can see there are queues.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I think on that front, we have to help the GPs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: GPs have given feedback to us that the patients either have mild or no symptoms.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They had self-tested, got a positive result and decided, "I had better see a GP, either to get an MC or some ART kits from the doctors." Many of them also worry about travel.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If they have to go through a PCR test while travelling, they like to say, "I register a positive result, but I am a recovered shedder".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They want to show that, actually, they have had COVID-19, they are shedders and they have recovered.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, for various reasons, people are visiting doctors and GPs, not because they are very sick.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From there, they can also withdraw ART kits.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What they will not get is a doctor's MC because, for that, you would have to see a doctor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, that way, I hope we can divert many of the very mild cases away from GP clinics into the QTCs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have about 200 QTCs now, all over, including in malls.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the findings that adolescents and children have a higher COVID-19 Omicron infection rate than older age groups, does the Senior Minister of State agree that it is better for them to get vaccinated with the Sinovac vaccine, than remain unvaccinated?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I recognise that it is generally better for them to get the Pfizer vaccine because it is more efficacious.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, these adolescents have chosen not to for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, from the residents I have met, either they or their parents have a preference for non-mRNA vaccines and are unlikely to change their stance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, why not approve the Sinovac vaccine for adolescents so that they will get vaccinated and our population can reach closer to a full vaccination rate earlier?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Jurisdictions like China and Hong Kong have already approved it for those aged three and above.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, what are the residual safety concerns to it becoming generally available for children and adolescents?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Nothing is completely absolutely safe or absolutely unsafe.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is about the relative risk and the relative benefit.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The individuals under the age of 17 who are getting the non-mRNA vaccines – currently, the Sinovac-CoronaVac vaccines – in those circumstances, because they are medically ineligible for the mRNA vaccines, the benefits of being vaccinated with any vaccine are, indeed, outweighed by the risks and safety concerns that currently exists for those vaccines, and weighed up against the risk of getting a Coronavirus infection.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But for the others who are not medically ineligible, the safety and efficacy data are quite clear.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Therefore, we would continue to recommend for them an mRNA vaccine.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because it is not just about their risks and their immunity at this point in time, but over the next few months, as the pandemic continues to be a challenge for us and around the world, we have to think about how quickly their immunity will wane, what would be their ability to deal with the future waves or even this existing wave as it makes its way through our society.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we continue to recommend the mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As I have explained, we are trying to bring in other options for these individuals in the near future.
